title.narrative: Restoring women, youth and health services In Iraq

description.narrative:
Iraq is suffering one of the most protracted humanitarian emergencies in the region. The humanitarian context facing Iraq in 2022 has significantly changed in recent years. While humanitarian needs in Iraq continue to be primarily driven by the effects of conflict and displacement, COVID-19 presented an additional shock in 2020. The impact of COVID-19—particularly the economic downturn caused by the deterioration of oil prices—have resulted in loss of livelihoods, while at the same time, the restriction in movements has disrupted access to services and increased protection and GBV risks. These conditions have had a significant socio-economic impact on the Iraqi population as a whole and have increased humanitarian needs especially among conflict-affected populations, particularly in out-of-camp and return locations. In addition, the closure of most of the camps for internally displaced persons (IDPs) have created disruption of services and have necessitated radical shifts in operations for humanitarian actors.
Considering these unexpected changes, humanitarian actors in Iraq has no longer primarily focus on servicing the needs of IDPs living in camps. The response mostly concentrates on the needs of vulnerable IDPs and returnees, the majority of whom are in out-of-camp locations. The needs of these populations can be less visible, but are often more acute with more severe implications, which are harder to address. Humanitarian need is expected to expand, and projections indicate poverty will increase between 14.4 to 18.7 percentage points. Conflict and military operations have also affected the public social services, including the survivors centred GBV services and women centres. Infrastructure, particularly the health system, remains adversely affected by the crisis. Although Iraq has made improvements in legal and policy frameworks to advance the empowerment of women and gender equality, still harmful.
The population of Iraq is estimated at 40 million, with 28 percent between 15-29 years old. The annual population growth rate is 2.8 percent, with the population projected to reach 50 million by 2030. While the recently conducted National Adolescent and Youth survey 2019, the net school enrolment rate for males and females was 94%; this goes down to 55% in secondary 28% in higher education. Looking at the unemployment, 27.5% of youth aged 15-24 years were unemployed at the time when the survey was conducted.
The status of youth in the country is very marginalized, due to the protracted crisis and was aggravated during the pandemic. This situation has increased the emotional, psychological, and mental health problems for adolescents and youth which in many cases led to suicidal attempts due to frustration and disappointment. The challenges of young people in general and youth with disabilities are also exacerbated, with protection issues due to the post humanitarian crisis context. There are no tailored programmes offered by the government where youth can get life skills, information and counselling services. Nonetheless, the youth centres of the Ministry of Youth and Sport and vocational training centres of the Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs (MOLSA) are offering only recreational activities and some conventional vocational courses that may not empower youth, help them in building their career or not making them future entrepreneurs or leaders. However, centres have a huge potential to engage adolescents and youth with disabilities in life skills education/reproductive health education, entrepreneurship, and leadership programmes for inclusion and socio-economic empowerment.
The project aims to identify, design, and rehabilitate in partnership with UNFPA women centres and youth centres used by women and by young people with disabilities aged 10-24 years to facilitate their movement and secure their safety and comfortability, and strengthen the connectivity and cohesion among communities. The project also aims to rehabilitate health facilities at the hospitals that provides delivery and caesarean section services, which all of them suffer from shortage of equipment, human resources to provide quality health services. The locations will be identified in coordination with the relevant local authorities.
The goal of the proposed response is to support the development of area-based recovery plan that through a joint effort facilitates the services for the most vulnerable people especially GBV survivors and young people with disabilities. UN-Habitat ensures that any engagement or collaboration with beneficiaries, national or international organizations will be based on the “Do No Harm Principles” to prevent and mitigate any negative impact of actions on affected populations. UN Habitat will also ensure that the facilities that provide services are accessible to women and girls with disabilities.
